title: Why Smart Projects Take Twice as Long as Planned
alt_title_1: The 1994 Study Behind Every Missed Project Deadline
alt_title_2: Daniel Kahneman's Outside-View Fix for the Planning Fallacy
description_hook: In 1994, psychologists Roger Buehler, Dale Griffin, and Michael Ross measured why intelligent people systematically underestimate completion times. Here is how Daniel Kahneman's Reference Class Forecasting fixes broken schedules.

scenes.headline: Why 'Two-Week' Sprints Turn Into Five Weeks
scenes.stat_label: TYPICAL SHARE FINISHING BY OWN ESTIMATE
bullets: Even experienced builders repeat optimistic deadline errors
Intelligence alone does not cure schedule blindness
scenes.narration: Why do intelligent, experienced professionals estimate a two-week project timeline and routinely finish five weeks later?
scenes.source: Buehler, Griffin & Ross, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1994)

scenes.headline: Buehler, Griffin & Ross's 1994 Thesis Study
bullets: Students predicted 34 days; actual average hit 55.5 days
Even their 'worst-case' estimates averaged only 49 days
scenes.narration: In a 1994 study, psychologists Roger Buehler, Dale Griffin, and Michael Ross asked honors students when their theses would finish. Students predicted thirty-four days on average, yet actual completion took nearly fifty-six.
scenes.source: Buehler, Griffin & Ross, JPSP, Vol. 67, No. 3 (1994)

scenes.headline: Inside View Fantasy vs Real-World Friction
scenes.left_body: Pictures zero interruptions, zero bugs, and best-case focus
scenes.right_body: Anchors on historical base rates of past comparable projects
scenes.narration: Daniel Kahneman traced this planning fallacy to the Inside View: your brain pictures an uninterrupted best-case sprint while ignoring sick days, scope changes, and hidden dependencies.
scenes.source: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011)

scenes.headline: Reference Class Forecasting + 1.5x Buffer
scenes.stat_subtext: Historical median duration x 1.5 buffer -> calm on-time shipping
scenes.narration: Use Kahneman's Reference Class Forecasting instead: check how long your last three similar projects actually took from start to finish, then multiply your optimistic estimate by one point five.
scenes.source: Lovallo & Kahneman, Harvard Business Review (2003); 1.5x buffer is practical advice

scenes.headline: Under-Promise on Dates, Over-Deliver on Craft
bullets: Log actual completion times to calibrate future quotes
Calm buffers turn rushed panic into trusted execution
scenes.narration: Price real-world friction into your calendar upfront so you hit deadlines calmly and protect your reputation.
scenes.source: Mind & Margin rule of thumb (advice, not a study)
